conclusion.label: rejects

report:
### Conclusion

High-quality clinical evidence indicates that saw palmetto (*Serenoa repens*) does **not** significantly improve lower urinary tract symptoms associated with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) compared to placebo over the longer term.

### Summary of Evidence

1. **Cochrane Reviews**: Systematic reviews demonstrate that saw palmetto, alone or combined with other phytotherapeutic agents, provides no clinically meaningful improvement in urologic symptoms or quality of life compared to placebo in either the short term (3–6 months) or long term (12–17+ months) (https://www.aafp.org/afp/2024/0500/cochrane-saw-palmetto-benign-prostatic-hyperplasia). Reviews of dozens of randomized controlled trials involving thousands of men further dispute its efficacy (https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/321911).
2. **Dose-Escalation Studies**: In the CAMUS clinical trial, researchers evaluated saw palmetto extract over 18 months, escalating doses from 320 mg/day up to triple the standard amount (960 mg/day). The trial concluded that saw palmetto failed to reduce lower urinary tract symptoms or objective measures of BPH superior to placebo at any dose level (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/1104439).
3. **Health Agency Findings**: Reviews summarized by the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH) conclude that saw palmetto has not been shown to be more effective than placebo for managing BPH symptoms (https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/providers/digest/spotlight-on-saw-palmetto-science).

In summary, rigorous clinical trials demonstrate that saw palmetto offers no significant long-term benefit over placebo for BPH symptom relief.
